speaker: A
text: Welcome to Benefits Unlocked, brought to you by HealthEquity — the nation's largest health savings account platform, trusted by nearly 10 million Americans to manage their HSAs, FSAs, COBRA, commuter benefits, and more. I'm your host, and today we're going to show you how to turn one line in your benefits enrollment email into the most powerful tax-free account you'll ever own.

speaker: B
text: Okay, so I literally just opened my benefits enrollment email this morning. I've been staring at it for an hour. And I'm about to click the same plan I had last year because the other option says 'high-deductible health plan' and that just sounds like it costs more.

speaker: A
text: Stop. Don't click yet. That line — high-deductible health plan — is the line I want to talk about for the next few minutes. Because what's hiding behind it is the most powerful tax-free account you'll ever own.

speaker: B
text: Tax-free account? I thought I was picking insurance.

speaker: A
text: You are. But when you pick the high-deductible health plan, you get access to something called an H-S-A — a Health Savings Account. And here's the line I want you to hold onto. The HSA is the only account in the American tax code where the money goes in tax-free, grows tax-free, and comes out tax-free — and it moves with you for life.

speaker: B
text: Tax-free three times? That sounds like something the IRS would never allow.

speaker: A
text: It is allowed. It's been allowed for over twenty years. And almost nobody uses the HSA the way it was designed. Most people who have heard of HSAs treat them as a spending account — money in, money out, doctor bills. That's accurate. It's also missing about ninety percent of what the account can do.

speaker: B
text: Okay, so what am I missing?

speaker: A
text: Let me give you a number first, because numbers land harder than concepts. If you contributed the 2026 individual maximum to your HSA — that's $4,400 a year — and you invested it at a seven percent average annual return for twenty years, you'd end up with approximately $180,000.

speaker: B
text: A hundred and eighty thousand dollars. In a health account.

speaker: A
text: $180,000. And every dollar of it is accessible tax-free for medical costs in retirement. Every dollar was put in tax-free. Every dollar grew tax-free. That is the cost of clicking the familiar plan and walking away from this. It's not abstract. It's a number.

speaker: B
text: I have been clicking the familiar plan for five years.

speaker: A
text: A lot of people have. That's why we're having this conversation.

speaker: B
text: Okay. Walk me through how the tax part actually works. Because three times tax-free sounds like marketing to me.

speaker: A
text: Fair. Let's do it with real numbers. First advantage — the money you put in is never subject to federal income tax. In most states, no state income tax either. If you contribute $4,400 in a year and you're in a combined thirty percent tax bracket, you've effectively saved $1,320 in taxes. Money that would have gone to the IRS is now sitting in your account.

speaker: B
text: So I save $1,320 just for moving the money into the right account.

speaker: A
text: Yes. Second advantage — the balance grows completely tax-free. If you invest it, your gains are never subject to capital gains tax. The interest, the dividends, the growth — none of it gets taxed, ever, as long as it stays in the account.

speaker: B
text: Okay, that's two. What's the third?

speaker: A
text: Third — when you spend HSA money on eligible health costs, the withdrawal isn't taxed either. A prescription, a dental cleaning, an eye exam, a hearing aid, a doctor's visit. You put it in without paying tax, it grew without paying tax, you took it out without paying tax.

speaker: B
text: Doesn't my 401(k) do this?

speaker: A
text: No. A 401(k) gives you the tax break going in, but taxes every dollar coming out. A Roth I-R-A taxes you going in but not coming out — that's two advantages, not three. Only the HSA does all three. The HSA is the only account in the American tax code where the money goes in tax-free, grows tax-free, and comes out tax-free — and it moves with you for life.

speaker: B
text: Okay. That's the second time you've said that exactly the same way. I'm starting to believe it.

speaker: A
text: Good. There are two more things you should know that almost nobody talks about. First — after age 65, you can use the HSA for anything. Not just healthcare. Anything. Non-medical withdrawals after 65 are taxed as ordinary income, exactly like a 401(k). But for medical costs, it stays tax-free.

speaker: B
text: So at 65 it becomes at least as good as a 401(k), and still better for healthcare.

speaker: A
text: Exactly. And second — the HSA has no required minimum distributions. A 401(k) forces you to start taking money out at age 73. Your HSA can sit and compound indefinitely. The IRS never makes you touch it.

speaker: B
text: That's a big deal. My dad just hit that age and he's stressed about pulling money he doesn't actually need.

speaker: A
text: It's a huge deal. One more piece — contributions made through payroll are also exempt from FICA. Those are the taxes that fund Social Security and Medicare. That's an extra 7.65 percent in savings on every dollar you contribute through payroll. A 401(k) doesn't give you that.

speaker: B
text: Okay. So why doesn't everyone do this?

speaker: A
text: Two reasons. The word 'deductible' scares people away from the plan in the first place. And the people who do open an HSA usually empty it every year — they treat it like a spending account, same as an FSA. They get one of the three tax advantages and throw away the other two.

speaker: B
text: What should they be doing instead?

speaker: A
text: Here's the move. Pay healthcare costs out of pocket when you can afford to. Let the HSA balance grow and invest it. And here's the part most people don't know — the IRS doesn't set a deadline for reimbursements. If you pay a $200 dental bill today and keep the receipt, you can reimburse yourself from your HSA five years from now, after the account has grown. The reimbursement is still tax-free.

speaker: B
text: So I could save my receipts for years and pull the money out later, tax-free?

speaker: A
text: Years. Decades. As long as you have the receipt and the expense was incurred after you opened the HSA. Think of it this way — unlike the FSA's use-it-or-lose-it rule, the HSA balance rolls over every year, indefinitely. It's the account that never expires.

speaker: B
text: Okay. So back to my enrollment email. What do I actually do?

speaker: A
text: Three steps. One — enroll in the high-deductible health plan. Two — open the HSA. Three — contribute at least enough to cover the deductible, and invest the rest. HealthEquity makes the investment piece simple. There's AutoPilot, which is fully automated, or GPS, which is guided. Both use low-cost Vanguard funds.

speaker: B
text: And the contribution limits again?

speaker: A
text: For 2026, $4,400 if it's just you. $8,750 if you're covering a family. If you're 55 or older, you can add another $1,000 on top. And here's the strategy — take the difference in monthly premium between the traditional plan and the high-deductible health plan and redirect that money straight into your HSA. Most years, the premium savings alone come close to covering typical out-of-pocket costs.

speaker: B
text: So I'm not actually losing money on the deductible. I'm just moving where the money sits.

speaker: A
text: You're redirecting premium savings into an account that's permanently yours. It belongs to you, not your employer, not your insurer. If you change jobs next year, the HSA comes with you. If you retire in thirty years, it's still there.

speaker: B
text: And it doubles as retirement money.

speaker: A
text: It doubles as retirement money. That's the retirement double-duty account — a liquid fund for near-term medical costs and a long-term investment vehicle for retirement healthcare spending, which is one of the largest and least predictable retirement expenses anyone faces.

speaker: B
text: Okay. I'm in. What happens if I wait another year?

speaker: A
text: You lose that year's tax savings and that year's growth. Permanently. The compounding clock doesn't start until you start contributing. Someone who starts at 25 and someone who starts at 35 with identical contributions don't end up in the same place — the ten extra years of growth is worth more than every contribution combined.

speaker: B
text: That's the cost of waiting.

speaker: A
text: That's the cost. So one more time, because this is the line worth remembering. The HSA is the only account in the American tax code where the money goes in tax-free, grows tax-free, and comes out tax-free — and it moves with you for life.

speaker: B
text: That's the line.

speaker: A
text: If you're ready to open your HSA today, go to healthequity.com. If your employer already uses HealthEquity — and there's a good chance they do — your account is waiting for you right now. It takes five minutes to get started. Don't let another enrollment season go by.

speaker: B
text: I'm opening mine tonight.
